speaker: Doctor
text: Hello, I am Dr. Agent. To help me understand what is going on with your little boy, could you please describe the nature of his feeding difficulties and how long you have noticed the abdominal distension?

speaker: Patient
text: The baby has been very fussy, feeding less than usual, and the abdomen looks distended. Crying gets worse when the belly is touched.

speaker: Doctor
text: Has he passed any stool recently, and if so, what did it look like? Also, has he had any vomiting or fever?

speaker: Patient
text: There has not been fever, vomiting, or diarrhea like a stomach infection. The baby was born at 39 weeks without birth complications.

speaker: Doctor
text: Has he passed any stool since birth, and if so, was it delayed or unusually large and foul-smelling? I need to know if there is a history of constipation or failure to thrive.

speaker: Patient
text: The baby did not seem to pass stool normally and the belly swelling has become more obvious. Feeding has clearly decreased over the past few days.

speaker: Doctor
text:
I need to confirm if he passed his meconium within the first 48 hours of life, as delayed passage is a key indicator. Please also let me know if you have noticed any explosive, watery stools after a digital rectal examination or if the abdomen feels hard to the touch.

The x-ray findings of dilated bowel segments with an air-filled rectum are classic for Hirschsprung disease, especially given the history of delayed meconium passage and abdominal distension. I will confirm this with a rectal suction biopsy, but the clinical picture is quite clear.
